fields.title: Klen: forty-six technicians and the old software
fields.summary: The new version must be rolled out by the end of the quarter. Decide how to transition the users.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you transition Zarechye to the new version?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Klen.
fields.brief/company: Klen is a fictional ticketing system for property management companies. The largest client is Zarechye PMC: 140 buildings, 9 dispatchers, 46 technicians.
fields.brief/context: The old version is a desktop app for dispatchers; technicians receive tickets by phone. The new version is a web dashboard for dispatchers and a mobile app for technicians. There is no one left to support the old version: the only developer who knew it resigned in December. You have one quarter for the transition.
fields.brief/objective: Transition Zarechye to the new version without disrupting ticket processing.
fields.brief/constraints: Three developers, one deployment specialist, part-time support. One quarter.
fields.brief/task: Choose a transition plan and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Data migration is the most visible part of a transition, but almost never the most dangerous. Work is disrupted by habits and a missing filter, not by the percentage of migrated records. Phased rollouts give you a chance to catch this on ten buildings instead of 140, keeping the old database active provides a rollback option, and training works best through the person everyone already goes to with questions.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
9 dispatchers working in shifts, average tenure of 6 years. They know the old software by heart and work almost without looking at the screen.

46 technicians: plumbers, electricians, carpenters. Aged 24 to 61. Everyone has a smartphone, but 11 people in the deployment specialist's survey said they don't use any apps except messengers.

Currently, tickets are sent to technicians by phone from the dispatcher, and completion is reported back via a phone call. Residents sign a paper work order.

There is Sergey at Zarechye—a technician everyone goes to with tech questions. He asked to see the new version himself.

Peak load is Monday and the first week of the heating season: up to 300 tickets per day compared to the usual 90.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: Status of the old and new versions
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Old version: software installed on each dispatcher's PC, database on a server in the PMC office. The developer who knew it resigned in December; there is no one to make changes.

New version: web dashboard and technician app. Tested on two small PMCs with 30 buildings each.

Data migration: 140 buildings, 12,400 apartments, 3 years of ticket history. A trial migration was done once: 96% of records migrated successfully, 4% had an empty "entrance" field—the cause was not investigated.

Address directory in the old version was filled manually, resulting in duplicate streets ("Lenina" and "Lenina St.").

Rollback to the old version is technically possible as long as both databases are active: this requires supporting two databases and manual reconciliation.

Parallel operation of both versions on a single database is impossible due to different structures.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Charges and personal accounts live in the PMC's billing system—a third-party solution updated once a quarter.

In the old version, dispatchers entered resident data manually. In the new version, it is planned to pull this from billing.

The billing provider delivers data exports once a day at night. No online queries are supported.

It is undecided what to do if a resident is not in the billing system (new owner, rented apartment): in the old version, the dispatcher simply typed the name manually.

It is undecided which address version is the source of truth: billing has clean addresses, while Klen has duplicates.

The billing provider responds to emails in 3–5 days. No test access has been provided yet.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
At another PMC last year, the transition was done overnight. In the morning, dispatchers couldn't find the "overdue" filter they were used to, and spent half the day logging tickets in notebooks. It took a week to restore that day's tickets.

Training back then was done via a webinar three days before the switch: 4 out of 11 dispatchers attended, and two watched the recording.

The deployment specialist says teaching technicians via webinars is useless: "They won't even open it."

The heating season in this city starts on October 15—it is currently July, but the quarter ends on September 30.

Part-time support: currently 20–30 tickets per week across all clients.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Phased rollout with rollback options and on-the-job training
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Transition in phases: first a few buildings and one champion technician, then groups. Train users during actual tasks rather than via webinars. Agree on billing integration rules beforehand.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
First wave: 10 buildings, two dispatchers, Sergey, and four technicians for two weeks.
Three issues surface: 4% of addresses have an empty "entrance" field (technicians don't know where to go), duplicate streets create two cards for the same building, and the "overdue" filter is missing in the new version—the very issue that stalled the previous transition.
All three are fixed before the second wave. Sergey trains the other technicians himself in their own language; the deployment specialist only visits those who still struggle.
You resolve billing rules in advance via email: the billing address is the source of truth; if a resident is missing from the export, manual entry with a tag is allowed.
The final wave ends on September 12, a month before the heating season. You keep the old database active until the end of October.
Support tickets for the quarter: 60, spread over weeks.
Compromise: you lived with two versions for three months and had to explain to the client why it took so long.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Migrate data over the weekend; everyone starts using the new version on Monday. Fast, cheap, no need to maintain two systems.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The switch happens on Sunday night—right before Monday, a peak day when tickets triple.
At 9 AM, the same issue as the previous PMC surfaces: the "overdue" filter is missing. Plus, 4% of addresses have no entrance, and duplicate streets cause confusion—technicians call dispatchers to clarify, and dispatchers call you.
By noon, some tickets are logged in notebooks. A rollback is technically possible, but no one makes the decision: data is already in the new database and missing from the old one.
For a week, support is busy only with Zarechye. The PMC director demands written explanations.
Eventually, it works, but trust is lost, and talks about transitioning the second client are postponed for six months.
Compromise: saved on parallel operations but paid with a week of chaos on a peak day.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Train everyone, then switch on a set date
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Train dispatchers and technicians, distribute instructions, and set a transition date in one month—people will be prepared.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The webinar for dispatchers attracts 5 out of 9 people. Technicians, as the deployment specialist warned, open neither the recording nor the instructions: only 7 out of 46 opened them.
The switch on the set date goes smoother than it could have: dispatchers who attended the webinar manage.
But technical surprises remain—empty entrances and duplicate streets surface on the very first day because no one tested the data in real work.
Technicians learn in the field by calling each other; Sergey becomes the help center anyway—but spontaneously and without your support.
Compromise: training was confused with testing; people were prepared for a system that hadn't been tested on their actual data.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Without resident data, the new version is incomplete. Build the integration first, then transition users in a single day in September.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Correspondence with the billing provider takes six weeks: replies arrive every 3–5 days, and test access is granted in mid-August.
The integration succeeds, and you make the right decision about addresses—billing is the source of truth.
However, only three weeks remain for the user transition, and it happens in a single day on September 24 because the quarter is ending.
Everything that would have been caught in the first wave surfaces for everyone at once: entrances, duplicates, and the missing filter.
There are three weeks left before the heating season, and dispatchers work at half capacity during the first week.
Compromise: technically everything is done right, but no time was left for people—even though they were the main risk.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Work order chosen by importance rather than cost of delay and size
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Release is assembled from ready-made pieces and does not allow completing the task end-to-end
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Risk is identified, but lacks a trigger, response plan, and owner
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Undecided whose data is the source of truth and what happens if one side is unavailable
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Transition is planned as a single switchover date without phases or rollback options
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Training is reduced to instructions instead of on-the-job guidance
